findings.paper_title: Minutes Public Pack, 26/03/2026 Standards & Audit Sub Board
findings.headline: Shared service staffing has identified vulnerabilities and attendance issues
findings.detail: The Standards & Audit Sub Board has noted that staffing in shared services has vulnerabilities and experiences attendance issues, which create an acknowledged service risk tracked as the Loss of Key Staff Strategic Risk.
findings.matters: Shared services support core council functions; staffing gaps could affect service delivery across multiple council operations and financial management.
findings.quote: All recognized that shared service staffing has vulnerabilities and there are sometimes issues with attendance which creates a risk covered by the Loss of Key Staff Strategic Risk

findings.paper_title: Minutes Public Pack, 26/03/2026 Standards & Audit Sub Board
findings.headline: Current IT staffing levels below requirements despite business case inclusion
findings.detail: The council acknowledges insufficient IT manpower is currently in place, although this staffing need has been built into the business case for the IT Improvement Programme. Specialist requirements have been identified and Microsoft licensing enhancements are being explored.
findings.matters: A gap between planned and actual staffing creates delivery risk; if staffing numbers don't materialise, critical infrastructure improvements including cyber risk remediation could be delayed.
findings.quote: although sufficient manpower was not currently in place it was built into the business case and some specialist requirement had been identified

findings.paper_title: Minutes Public Pack, 26/03/2026 Standards & Audit Sub Board
findings.headline: Unsupported Windows 10 systems identified as creating a cyber risk
findings.detail: The council has desktop and laptop computers still running unsupported Windows 10, which the Head of IT has explicitly flagged as creating a cyber security risk. A budget bid focuses on this as a critical requirement for replacement or upgrade.
findings.matters: Cyber vulnerabilities from unsupported systems create material operational and business continuity risk; a breach could disrupt services and require expensive remediation.
findings.quote: a bid in the budget focused on critical requirements such as desk top and laptops still on now unsupported Windows 10 creating a cyber risk

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Annual Governance Statement GBC 2526 FINAL
findings.headline: Workforce capacity severely stretched by Local Government Reorganisation on a lean organisation
findings.detail: The council is 'a small and very lean organisation' with 'many staff covering multiple responsibilities.' LGR commitments will 'place significant demands on existing senior staff' and 'create additional capacity pressures' that could impact governance delivery.
findings.matters: A lean workforce already stretched thin, facing simultaneous financial transformation and LGR delivery, creates material execution risk across financial, governance and service priorities.
findings.quote: These ongoing workstreams will continue to create additional capacity pressures for a Council that already relies on a lean workforce, with many staff covering multiple responsibilities.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Annual Governance Statement GBC 2526 FINAL
findings.headline: Increasing limited assurance internal audit findings with poor follow-up completion
findings.detail: The council identifies 'Increasing number of Limited Assurance internal audits and reduction in follow up actions being completed' as a significant governance issue. Improvement initiatives were 'not as effective as desired.' Audit tracking and section performance management to be introduced.
findings.matters: Increasing limited assurance findings indicate control environment weakening; poor follow-up means issues persist, reflecting governance control concerns.
findings.quote: Increasing number of Limited Assurance internal audits and reduction in follow up actions being completed

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Annual Governance Statement GBC 2526 FINAL
findings.headline: Housing Regulator issued C4 judgement for significant governance failures
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing issued a C4 judgement, which the council explicitly identifies as 'a significant governance issue because of the seriousness of the weaknesses identified and the need for sustained regulatory improvement.' Action plan developed with regular regulator meetings.
findings.matters: A C4 judgement indicates serious deficiencies in housing governance and compliance, reflecting broader governance quality concerns and creating ongoing regulatory risk.
findings.quote: The Council was inspected by the Regulator of Social Housing, which resulted in a C4 judgement. This represented a significant governance issue because of the seriousness of the weaknesses identified and the need for sustained regulatory improvement.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Annual Governance Statement GBC 2526 FINAL
findings.headline: Senior management vacancies in finance, regeneration and procurement under review
findings.detail: Beyond the S151 Officer vacancy, the council has additional senior roles vacant in regeneration, finance and procurement undergoing recruitment review. Housing & Property structure is also under review to address regulatory concerns.
findings.matters: Multiple vacancies in finance and regeneration leadership during transformation increases execution risk on savings and service delivery changes.
findings.quote: Other senior roles in regeneration, finance and procurement are currently vacant and are being reviewed with a view to recruitment.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Annual Governance Statement GBC 2526 FINAL
findings.headline: Section 151 Officer post vacant during critical transformation period
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer (chief finance officer) role is vacant as of June 2026 with interim recruitment underway. The previous incumbent stepped back due to LGR commitments. This vacancy coincides with urgent financial transformation.
findings.matters: The Section 151 Officer is the statutory chief finance officer. Vacancy in this role during financial crisis and transformation amplifies execution risk.
findings.quote: As at June 2026, interim recruitment to the Section 151 Officer role was under way.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Annual Governance Statement GBC 2526 FINAL
findings.headline: Planned savings are not being delivered on schedule, exacerbating budget pressures
findings.detail: The council identifies that 'the delivery of necessary savings not being achieved at the speed envisaged' is exacerbating budget pressures. This slippage in savings execution undermines the financial assumptions built into medium-term plans.
findings.matters: Savings plans falling behind schedule indicate either over-optimistic planning or operational execution challenges; both signal transformation risk.
findings.quote: This situation is exacerbated by the delivery of necessary savings not being achieved at the speed envisaged, coupled with the inclusion of other costs of a political priority that, whilst avoidable, are not considered desirable.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Annual Governance Statement GBC 2526 FINAL
findings.headline: 2026/27 budget requires £1.36m draw on Revenue Financing Reserve to balance
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget requires the council to draw £1.36m from its Revenue Financing Reserve to achieve balance. This is a structural interim measure while transformation is planned.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdowns signal ongoing structural imbalance; sustained drawdowns accelerate reserve depletion and constrain financial flexibility.
findings.quote: The overall financial impact of the Budget Proposal for 2026/27 requires a draw on the Revenue Financing Reserve of £1.36m

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Annual Governance Statement GBC 2526 FINAL
findings.headline: Structural budget deficit of £3.3m by 2029/30 (22% of current spending) will require significant service transformation and reduction
findings.detail: The council forecasts a structural deficit of £3.3m by 2029/30, representing almost 22% of current net spending. The Budget Paper explicitly states this will require 'significant transformation of services, improvements in productivity, and the application of modern technology, alongside regrettable reductions in services to residents.'
findings.matters: A structural deficit of 22% of spending signals acute financial sustainability concerns and indicates the likelihood of material service cuts or further borrowing.
findings.figures: £3.3m deficit by 2029/30; almost 22% of current net spending
findings.quote: A deficit of £3.3m represents almost 22% of current net spending, and it is inevitable that savings of that scale will require a significant transformation of services, improvements in productivity, and the application of modern technology, alongside regrettable reductions in services to residents.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Annual Audit Report and Opinion 202526
findings.headline: 64% of agreed audit actions remain open or in progress; governance measure introduced to enforce compliance
findings.detail: Audits identify risks; management agree to fix them. In 2025/26, only 36% of followed-up actions were actually completed and verified. 64% remained either open or in progress. The report flags this as 'concerning from an internal control and overall corporate governance perspective'. Management has now introduced compulsory action tracking reviewed by CMT and is summoning Section Heads with poor progress to the Standards & Audit Sub Board.
findings.matters: If councils don't implement audit recommendations, risks accumulate. This indicates weak management discipline around financial and operational controls, a material concern for lenders.
findings.figures: 36% of follow-ups closed and verified (vs 24% in 2024/25); 60% in progress; 4% open; 53 out of 83 tracked exceptions remain outstanding
findings.quote: While this represents a better position than 2024/25, there remains a significant number of actions outstanding across the Authority, indicating that timely implementation of agreed actions is still an area requiring continued management focus. A key to good governance is management's response to risks identified in audit and, although the 2025/26 results show improvement, the volume of outstanding actions remains concerning from an internal control and overall corporate governance perspective.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Annual Audit Report and Opinion 202526
findings.headline: Seven IT audits rated Limited Assurance with systematic failure to remediate; IT department overhaul underway
findings.detail: IT has 7 of the 13 Limited Assurance audits. Follow-ups showed 'limited progress' on agreed actions. The Strategic Head of IT was forced to present a paper to the Standards & Audit Sub Board in March 2026 confirming that all previous agreed actions were 'no longer fit for purpose' and restarting with a new plan. This signals systematic failure in a critical infrastructure area.
findings.matters: IT failures can disable financial systems, payroll, and council operations. The fact that management had to scrap previous remediation plans suggests control failures are deeper than initially thought.
findings.figures: 7 of 13 Limited Assurance audits in IT department; 5 of 6 IT follow-ups remained at Limited Assurance with no change; 2 qualified IT auditors on team, one retiring soon
findings.quote: This is a cause for concern for the Authority due to the significant number of risks raised in the department, especially as IT risks can cause significant disruption to the entire Council. The Strategic Head of IT brought a paper to the Standards and Audit Sub Board in March 2026 outlining that the initial agreed actions by the previous Section Head were deemed no longer fit for purpose and, as such, a new action plan has been drafted.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Annual Audit Report and Opinion 202526
findings.headline: Annual audit opinion remains at Limited Assurance, below acceptable standard
findings.detail: Gosport's overall audit opinion is Limited Assurance, indicating significant weaknesses in the council's control environment. The report explicitly notes this level is 'still below an acceptable standard' despite marginal improvements in action completion. The rating reflects 13 audits rated Limited Assurance during the year and ongoing failure to implement agreed audit actions.
findings.matters: Limited Assurance means the council's financial and operational controls have material weaknesses. Lenders need to understand that control failures create financial and reputational risk.
findings.figures: 13 Limited Assurance audits in 2025/26; 6 Limited Assurance audits within the year; 42 High Risk exceptions and 34 Medium Risk exceptions remain open
findings.quote: the annual audit opinion for 2025/26 will remain at Limited Assurance, noting that while there has been an improvement in the completion of actions relating to risks, this level is still below an acceptable standard

findings.headline: Limited Assurance audit opinion continues for second consecutive year despite noted improvements.
findings.detail: The Internal Audit Annual Opinion for 2025/26 provides Limited Assurance on the internal control framework, maintaining the same assurance level as 2024/25. Although improvements have been noted, the council has not achieved Reasonable Assurance, indicating persistent weaknesses in internal controls.
findings.matters: Continued Limited Assurance means control weaknesses persist and increase risk to financial management and governance; a second consecutive year suggests systemic rather than transitional issues.
findings.quote: The Board is asked to note the Internal Audit Annual Opinion 2025/26, which provides Limited Assurance on the internal control framework. This continues the assurance level from 2024/25; however, improvements have been noted.

findings.paper_title: Finance Board paper - Additional Budget Savings Final
findings.headline: Council redirecting underspent grants and all new savings into Revenue Financing Reserve
findings.detail: A £6,442 balance from 2025/26 Community Grants is being transferred to the Revenue Financing Reserve, and all £31,442 of proposed savings are similarly directed to the Reserve rather than offsetting recurrent spend or supporting other services.
findings.matters: Proactive reserve building when facing a £100,000 savings commitment suggests the council is concerned about financial resilience and expects continued pressure on the revenue budget.
findings.figures: Community Grants carryover £6,442; total savings to Revenue Financing Reserve £31,442
findings.quote: The proposed savings of £31,442 will be transferred into the Revenue Financing Reserve if approved.

findings.paper_title: Finance Board paper - Additional Budget Savings Final
findings.headline: Discretionary service cuts: ending Gosport in Bloom and cutting community event budgets
findings.detail: The council is removing the £5,000 Gosport in Bloom budget entirely and reducing events budget by £20,000, cutting community discretionary services rather than operational efficiency. The paper notes the programme will cease and work must start immediately to notify stakeholders.
findings.matters: Service cuts rather than efficiency gains suggest the budget gap is structural. Discretionary spending reductions indicate limited easy savings remain and more difficult decisions lie ahead in the Transformation Plan.
findings.figures: Gosport in Bloom removal £5,000; Events budget reduction £20,000
findings.quote: The £5,000 reduction will result in the Gosport Schools in Bloom and Gosport in Bloom events coming to an end.

findings.paper_title: Finance Board paper - Additional Budget Savings Final
findings.headline: Remaining £68,558 of savings depends on Transformation Plan not yet approved by Full Council
findings.detail: Subsequent papers identifying the remaining £68,558 will be informed by the Council's Transformation Plan, which has not yet been approved. This creates uncertainty about how two-thirds of the savings commitment will be delivered and whether alternative scenarios are being considered.
findings.matters: A lender assessing budget sustainability needs a funded delivery mechanism. Approving a savings commitment before the plan to deliver it creates execution risk and suggests the council may lack contingency if the plan is delayed or modified.
findings.quote: subsequent papers to follow that will identify the remaining balance of the £100,000 savings commitment. These further savings will be informed by the Council's Transformation Plan, to be approved by Full Council

findings.paper_title: Finance Board paper - Additional Budget Savings Final
findings.headline: Only £31,442 of £100,000 additional savings commitment has been identified, leaving £68,558 still to find
findings.detail: The Council Leader publicly committed on 4 March to identify £100,000 in additional budget savings for 2026/27. This paper proposes only £31,442 through events budget reduction (£20,000), Community Grants carryover (£6,442), and ending Gosport in Bloom (£5,000). The remaining £68,558 is acknowledged as outstanding and unidentified.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence the council can execute on public financial commitments. An incomplete savings plan mid-year signals either inadequate budget planning or difficulty identifying cuts without service reduction.
findings.figures: Savings Commitment £100,000; Proposed savings £31,442 (Events £20,000, Community Grants balance £6,442, Gosport in Bloom £5,000); Outstanding £68,558
findings.quote: At the Full Council meeting on 4 March 2026, the Leader provided an assurance that a paper would be brought to the P&O Board to identify a further £100,000 in budget savings for the financial year 2026/27. Savings Commitment Outstanding £68,558

findings.headline: Internal financial reserves halving in one year; Council depleting its borrowing buffer
findings.detail: The under-borrowing position (the difference between the Council's capital borrowing requirement and actual external borrowing, representing internal resources available to temporarily fund capital) has fallen from £21.8m to £13.5m in 12 months. Forecasts show continued decline to £11.5m by 2027/28. This means the Council's cash reserves are running down faster than historical norms and it will become increasingly reliant on external credit markets.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand whether the Council retains sufficient reserves to absorb cash flow pressures or unexpected costs. Rapidly depleting internal resources reduce financial flexibility and increase dependence on continued access to debt markets at acceptable rates.
findings.quote: By 31 March 2026, the Council expects to be under‑borrowed by £13.5 million, which is £9.2 million less than the under‑borrowing position reported the previous year

findings.headline: External debt jumped £12 million in one year and continues rising toward £74 million
findings.detail: The Council's external loans increased from £59.6m (2024/25 actual) to £70.2m (2025/26 revised) and are forecast to reach £73.7m by March 2027. This represents rapid growth in debt over two years driven by capital programme funding. Debt is forecast to then stabilize and begin declining.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand why external debt is accelerating and whether the Council can service this level of borrowing from revenue. Rising debt also reduces the Council's financial headroom.
findings.quote: The Council expects to hold around £71 million of loans at 31 March 2026, an increase of £12 million from the previous year

findings.headline: Business Rates Retention revenue falls 64% with shift toward government grant dependency
findings.detail: Business Rates Retention income falls from £5,714,700 in 2025/26 revised to £2,051,690 in 2026/27—a decline of £3,663,010 or 64%. The council offsets this by increasing government grants from £2,037,620 to £4,923,700 (141% increase). The document does not explain the cause of the business rates collapse.
findings.matters: A dramatic drop in a traditionally predictable revenue source, replaced by discretionary government grants, increases the council's vulnerability to central policy changes and reduces financial autonomy.
findings.figures: Business Rates Retention: £5,714,700 (2025/26 revised) to £2,051,690 (2026/27), a drop of £3,663,010
findings.quote: BUSINESS RATES RETENTION (5,754,340)      (5,714,700)      (2,051,690)

findings.headline: Revenue Financing Reserve drawn down by £1.36m in 2026/27 to support operational budget
findings.detail: The council is transferring £1,359,530 FROM its Revenue Financing Reserve in 2026/27 to balance the budget, up significantly from £227,660 transferred in 2025/26 revised. Additionally, the Stability and Resilience Reserve is being drawn down by £537,410. These transfers total nearly £1.9m in reserve depletion.
findings.matters: Drawing reserves to fund recurring operations indicates the council's day-to-day revenue is insufficient to cover day-to-day spending. This erodes financial buffers available for unexpected costs, revenue shortfalls, or service emergencies.
findings.figures: Revenue Financing Reserve 2026/27 transfer: (£1,359,530); Stability and Resilience Reserve transfer: (£537,410)
findings.quote: The Streetscene review was completed in 2024/25 with the cost of redundancy and pension strain included above are being funded from the Revenue Financing Reserves.

findings.headline: Waste collection costs rising 29% from October 2026 due to mandatory food waste separation rollout
findings.detail: The waste budget increases from £2,272,120 to £2,930,620 (£658,500 or 29% growth). This is driven by a statutory requirement to introduce separate weekly food waste collection starting October 2026, requiring purchase and distribution of new collection containers to every household.
findings.matters: This is a locked-in statutory service expansion with a fixed implementation date, creating a material one-time cost and reducing the council's budget flexibility.
findings.figures: Waste 2026/27 budget £2,930,620, up from £2,272,120 in 2025/26 revised; includes new equipment and collection costs
findings.quote: Preparations are underway for the separate collection of Food Waste which will be rolled out to all residents in October 2026. Households will be provided with 5 litre kitchen Caddies and either 23 litre containers or 140 litre wheeled bins which will be placed out at the kerbside for collection on a weekly basis.

findings.headline: Homelessness service pressures driving 33% budget increase amid government-mandated obligations
findings.detail: The homelessness budget rises from £934,000 (2025/26 revised) to £1,241,430 (2026/27), an increase of £307,430. The council identifies this as driven by legislative and policy additions from central government: the Ending Rough Sleeping strategy, the Domestic Abuse Act 2023, and the Renters Reform Act 2025, alongside ongoing pressures from cost-of-living impacts and resettlement schemes.
findings.matters: This is a statutory service where costs are rising faster than council resources, driven by government mandate rather than local choice. Lenders need to understand whether councils can absorb such mandated cost growth without reducing other services.
findings.figures: Homelessness 2026/27 budget £1,241,430 vs £934,000 in 2025/26 revised (increase of £307,430 or 33%)
findings.quote: This service is under increasing pressures through additionals burdens being added from Government, such as the introduction of the Ending Rough Sleeping ofr Good strategy in 2022, the Domestic Abuse Act 2023 & more recently the Renters Reform Act 2025.

findings.headline: No reserves are planned to be drawn down across the three-year period despite projected deficits
findings.detail: The forecast line for 'Contribution to / (from) Reserves' shows zero for all three years. This means the council is not planning to use accumulated reserves to cover the projected budget gaps.
findings.matters: If deficits are real but no reserves are being deployed to cover them, this suggests either the reserves are restricted or unavailable, or the shortfalls will be closed through alternative means not detailed in this forecast.
findings.figures: Reserve contribution: 0 (shown as '-') for each year
findings.quote: CONTRIBUTION TO / (FROM) RESERVES -  -  -

findings.headline: Pension costs are forecast to increase from £657k to £1.9m, rising 190% over three years
findings.detail: Pension contributions are projected to rise from £657k in 2026/27 to £1,904k in 2028/29, adding £1.2m to annual costs by year three. This is a structural, fixed cost.
findings.matters: Rising pension obligations indicate growing liabilities that cannot be easily controlled and reduce the council's financial flexibility.

findings.headline: Government grants are projected to fall from £3.4m to £1.1m—a 69% reduction by 2028/29
findings.detail: Central government funding shows £3,514k in 2026/27, reducing to £3,428k in 2027/28, then dropping sharply to £1,071k in 2028/29. This represents a loss of £2.4m year-on-year by year three compared to 2027/28 levels. The document does not explain the reason for this sharp reduction.
findings.matters: Major reductions in government funding directly reduce available resources and require offsetting savings or service changes, creating significant financial pressure.
findings.quote: GOVERNMENT GRANTS (SEE BELOW) (3,514) (3,428) (1,071)

findings.headline: Annual budget deficits of £2.8-3.3m are projected, with savings targets of only £300-1,500k per year
findings.detail: The forecast shows budget deficits of £2,787k (2026/27), £3,174k (2027/28), and £3,294k (2028/29). Against these, the council plans in-year savings of £1,500k, £1,500k, and £300k respectively. The in-year savings targets do not cover the full deficit in any year, leaving a shortfall that must be covered by other means.
findings.matters: Multi-year deficits indicate the council is spending beyond its means and requires either additional funding sources, service reductions, reserves drawdown, or further savings not yet identified.

findings.headline: PWLB long-term borrowing rates now 6%+ against council's current 3.72% average, creating refinancing risk
findings.detail: As at 6 February 2026, PWLB long-term borrowing rates range from 6.08% (50-year) to 6.28% (30-year). The council currently holds £66m of borrowing at 3.72% average. When existing debt matures and requires refinancing, the council will face substantially higher interest costs.
findings.matters: Refinancing the council's £66m existing debt at current PWLB rates would materially increase annual financing charges and worsen revenue budget sustainability
findings.figures: PWLB rates: 6.08% (50-year), 6.18% (20-year), 6.23% (40-year), 6.28% (30-year). Council's current portfolio: £66m at 3.72% average rate
findings.quote: As at 6 February 2026, indicative PWLB long‑term fixed rates were approximately 6.18% (20‑year), 6.28% (30‑year), 6.23% (40‑year) and 6.08% (50‑year).

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account financing costs rising to 30.3% of revenue stream in 2026/27
findings.detail: HRA net financing costs (interest and Minimum Revenue Provision) are rising from 29.2% in 2025/26 to 30.3% in 2026/27, continuing an upward trend from 28.0% in 2024/25. This means over 30 pence of every HRA revenue pound is committed to servicing existing debt rather than housing services or maintenance.
findings.matters: The HRA is ring-fenced; high financing costs compress the operating budget and constrain the council's ability to invest in housing maintenance, new build, or service improvements
findings.figures: HRA financing costs as percentage of revenue stream: 28.0% (2024/25), 29.2% (2025/26), 30.3% (2026/27), then 28.4% (2027/28) and 27.0% (2028/29)
findings.quote: % Net Financing Costs to Revenue Stream HRA 28.0% 29.2% 30.3% 28.4% 27.0%

findings.headline: Prudential borrowing planned to increase 69% to £3.2m in 2026/27, with underlying debt requirement rising by £2.6m
findings.detail: New capital borrowing is planned to increase from £1.9m (revised 2025/26) to £3.2m in 2026/27. The Capital Financing Requirement—the council's underlying need to borrow—is forecast to increase by £2.6m during 2026/27 alone, reaching £86.5m total. This represents a material acceleration in debt-financed capital investment.
findings.matters: A rapid increase in borrowing increases long-term debt obligations and exposes the council to refinancing risk as interest rates have risen significantly
findings.figures: Borrowing: £0.9m (2024/25 actual), £1.9m (2025/26 revised), £3.2m (2026/27 estimate). Total CFR: £83.6m, £84.4m, £86.5m for same years
findings.quote: The CFR is expected to increase by £2.585m during 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Summary of Service Budgets
findings.headline: Local taxation budget unexpectedly increased by £355,590 (158% increase)
findings.detail: Local taxation revised budget of £224,300 jumped to estimated £579,890 for 2026/27—a 158% increase with no narrative explanation in this summary.
findings.matters: This is an unusually large and unexplained budget jump for a single function; without context it raises questions about whether there is a cost pressure or administrative issue driving the change.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Summary of Service Budgets
findings.headline: Homelessness expenditure surging 33% year-on-year (£307,430 increase)
findings.detail: Housing board homelessness budget jumped from £934,000 (revised 2025/26) to £1,241,430 (2026/27 estimate), an increase of £307,430 representing 33% growth in a single year.
findings.matters: Sharp year-on-year growth in homelessness costs suggests escalating demand the council struggles to manage, a pressure that will persist if underlying demand is rising.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Summary of Service Budgets
findings.headline: Waste costs forecast £658,500 higher than revised budget (29% increase)
findings.detail: Waste budget increased from revised forecast of £2,272,120 to estimated £2,930,620, a variance of £658,500 between the revised and original estimate. This was not anticipated in the mid-year reforecast.
findings.matters: A 29% cost increase mid-forecast suggests either significant volume growth or cost inflation the council failed to anticipate, indicating potential loss of spending control.

findings.headline: Economic uncertainty makes forward LCTS demand unpredictable despite no government funding buffer
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that 'the current un-settled national economic situation makes it difficult to forecast LCTS caseload and expenditure with any degree of certainty.' Any increase in demand from worsening economic conditions falls entirely on the council's budget, with no government contribution.
findings.matters: Demand that cannot be reliably forecast combined with a fully unfunded commitment creates material budget risk and planning uncertainty.
findings.quote: The current un-settled national economic situation makes it difficult to forecast LCTS caseload and expenditure with any degree of certainty.

findings.headline: Rising LCTS caseload and an unfunded statutory obligation place continued pressure on the council's budget
findings.detail: Gosport's LCTS caseload has increased materially due to the UC managed migration programme, with working-age claimants rising from 2,007 (2023/24) to 3,323 (early 2026). The council receives no direct government funding for this statutory service, and estimated 2026/27 costs are £5,000,000, of which Gosport pays £588,000. The risk assessment explicitly identifies this as placing 'continued pressure on the Council's budget.'
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility of unfunded statutory obligations that are growing. LCTS costs fall entirely on the council's budget, and a 65% rise in claimants over two years creates forward budget risk.
findings.figures: Working-age caseload 2,007 (2023/24) to 3,323 (early 2026); total scheme cost £5,000,000; Gosport's share £588,000 (11.76%); actual 2024/25 spend £4,906,466; actual to January 2026 £4,919,195
findings.quote: No direct government funding is received by the Council for the costs of the LCTS scheme.

findings.headline: Over 60% of council tenants dependent on benefit assistance with income exposed to welfare policy changes
findings.detail: The council advised that over 60% of Gosport tenants receive some form of benefit assistance to pay rent. Whilst the autumn statement brought increases in help for tenants, this indicates substantial income dependency on welfare policy outside the council's control. Rents remain below comparable Housing Association and private sector levels.
findings.matters: High benefit dependency creates income volatility risk if government welfare policy changes, and suggests limited capacity to absorb rent or subsidy changes.
findings.quote: over 60% of GBC tenants receive some sort of benefit to assist in the paying of their rent

findings.headline: £625,000 improvement plan cost being funded from Housing Revenue Account reserves
findings.detail: To address the RSH inspection findings, the council is committing £625,000 for expert consultancy and additional temporary staff to develop a Comprehensive Improvement Plan. This is being funded from the New Build Reserve within HRA reserves. The Group Accountant noted that reserves are not fixed and could be used for unexpected costs, indicating they are being actively deployed rather than held as buffer.
findings.matters: Drawing down reserves for reactive compliance funding reduces financial flexibility and buffer against service pressures or policy changes in the housing service.
findings.quote: the Board endorses the additional financial resources at an estimated cost of £625,000 from the Housing Revenue Account reserves for expert consultancy and additional temporary staff

findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing inspection resulted in C4 grading with findings of very serious failings
findings.detail: The council's housing service was inspected by the Regulator of Social Housing and received a C4 grading. The board acknowledged very serious failings were identified. The council is now required to work intensively with the regulator to provide assurance of change and progress. Members were advised that only 7 of other councils inspected had received this grading, indicating this is a rare and serious outcome.
findings.matters: Regulatory failure in a major council service indicates serious governance and operational weaknesses that could affect service continuity and create reputational risk for a borrower.
findings.figures: C4 grading; only 7 of councils completed inspections had received same grading
findings.quote: Consideration was given to a report by the Head of Housing (HOH) updating the Board on the outcome of the Regulator of Social Housing (RSH) inspection, acknowledging the very serious failings identified

findings.headline: HRA financing costs peak at 30.3% of revenue in 2026/27
findings.detail: Housing revenue account financing costs are forecast to reach 30.3% of revenue in 2026/27, up from 29.2% in 2025/26. This is the highest point in the five-year planning period and represents significant pressure on HRA cash flow.
findings.matters: HRA financing costs above 30% constrain rent affordability and service investment in housing; such levels indicate structural financial pressure within the housing service.

findings.headline: External debt is planned to accumulate £14.1m over two years to £73.65m by 2026/27
findings.detail: External debt is forecast to rise from £59.55m (2024/25 actual) to £73.65m (2026/27 estimate), a 23% increase in debt stock. Debt then stabilizes with minimal further increases through 2028/29.
findings.matters: Material debt accumulation affects debt sustainability and creditworthiness; lenders assess whether accumulated debt can be serviced from the council's revenue base.

findings.headline: Planned borrowing of £3.2m in 2026/27 is followed by near-zero borrowing thereafter
findings.detail: Borrowing is forecast at £3.2m in 2026/27, aligned with the peak capital expenditure year, but then drops to £2k in 2027/28 and £0 in 2028/29. This sharp cessation suggests the major capital programmes are front-loaded or external funding sources are expected to meet future capital needs.
findings.matters: The abrupt end of borrowing requires explanation; it could indicate either sustainable capex frontloading or reliance on future grants that may not materialise.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure spikes to £26.9m in 2026/27 then drops sharply to £6.2m by 2028/29
findings.detail: Capital spending is forecast to jump 58% to £26.9m in 2026/27 from a revised £17.0m in 2025/26, then contract to £11.2m in 2027/28 and £6.2m in 2028/29. This uneven profile suggests either a major scheme completing in 2026/27 or frontloaded investment tied to external funding windows.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand what drives this capital peak and whether the revenue base can support the associated borrowing and ongoing debt servicing costs.

findings.headline: The council must deliver £3m in savings over three years but has not yet finalised the Transformation Plan needed to identify how these will be achieved.
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer states it is 'vital' that the council prepares 'a comprehensive and cohesive Transformation Plan' with full political and management support. The required savings are described as 'daunting due to its scale' (£1.5m in 2027/28, £1.5m in 2028/29, £0.3m in 2029/30). No detailed plan appears to be in place at budget approval, though the report references peer challenge insights, property strategy, and organisational redesign as potential sources.
findings.matters: Large-scale public sector transformation is difficult to execute. The council has already underdelivered against its 2026/27 savings target by £0.6m. Absence of a detailed plan at budget approval suggests savings targets are aspirational rather than committed, increasing the risk that forecast savings will not be delivered and reserve depletion will accelerate.
findings.quote: the Council has a 2 year time horizon to identify and deliver savings of £3m, this should be informed by a comprehensive and cohesive Transformation Plan that has the full support and commitment of both the Political Leadership of the Council and Senior Management. Whilst daunting due to its scale

findings.headline: The Government's Fair Funding Review has been 'negative for the Council', leaving funding cash flat for all non-homelessness services while unavoidable costs rise by double digits.
findings.detail: Government funding will increase only 5% over three years (2026/27-2028/29), but all of that increase is reserved for Homelessness, Rough Sleeping and Domestic Abuse. Funding for all other services is cash flat. Unavoidable cost pressures total over £2m in 2026/27 alone: pay +£0.5m, food waste +£0.4m, homelessness +£0.3m, contract uplifts +£0.4m. The council identifies this mismatch as 'the major contributory factor driving the Structural Budget Deficit'.
findings.matters: This is an external constraint entirely outside the council's control. With council tax capped at 2.99% and no discretion on pay or statutory services, the council has no mechanism to offset a structural imbalance between flat-cash funding and inflation-driven costs. Financial recovery depends entirely on service transformation, not improved funding.
findings.figures: 5% Government funding increase over 3 years (all for homelessness); other services cash flat; unavoidable costs: pay +£0.5m (3%), food waste +£0.4m, homelessness +£0.3m, contracts +£0.4m
findings.quote: With a Local Government Finance Settlement being cash flat for the majority of services and costs rising with inflation and demand generally, a structural financial imbalance arises. This is the major contributory factor driving the Structural Budget Deficit of the Council

findings.headline: The Revenue Financing Reserve will drop from £3.9m to £2.5m in one year and is forecast to reach its bare minimum (£1.045m) by 2029/30.
findings.detail: The council will withdraw £1.36m in 2026/27 and a further £1.461m over 2027-2030. The Section 151 Officer states: if savings targets are not met, 'the Reserve will be completely exhausted during 2027/28'. Even with successful savings delivery, the reserve reaches £1.045m by 2029/30, at the bare minimum threshold. This leaves virtually no buffer for financial shocks.
findings.matters: A reserves position this depleted severely limits the council's financial resilience. Any variance on planned savings—underspend, cost overrun, demand increase, or economic shock—could force the council to issue a section 114 notice triggering spending controls. Lenders need assurance of financial flexibility; this position offers none.
findings.quote: the Revenue Financing Reserve is the Council's barometer of its financial standing and resilience and based on the Council's current Structural Deficits, if left unattended, the Reserve will be completely exhausted during 2027/28.

findings.headline: Planned savings are underperforming, with only £0.4m delivered for 2026/27 against the £1m target—a £0.6m shortfall driving £1.36m reserve drawdown.
findings.detail: The council proposed £0.7m savings but added £0.275m in political priority costs (capital contributions to regeneration), resulting in only £0.4m net savings. This £0.6m shortfall against the previously approved £1m target is explicitly identified as a major factor in the need for the reserve withdrawal. Future savings mechanisms for the £3m required over 2027/28-2029/30 have not yet been detailed.
findings.matters: Underdelivery of savings by 60% in the current year raises execution risk for future forecasts. With no Transformation Plan yet finalised, the council depends entirely on delivering £3m in further savings to avoid reserve exhaustion—yet has already missed targets. Political priority spending competing with financial sustainability suggests governance pressures.
findings.figures: £0.7m proposed savings, £0.275m political priority costs added, net £0.4m vs £1m target (£0.6m shortfall); £0.6m variance drives £1.36m reserve drawdown
findings.quote: Savings for 2026/27 of £0.7m have been proposed alongside other proposed cost increases of a political priority of £0.275m which, in combination, have had the effect of reducing the net savings made to £0.4m.

findings.headline: Gosport faces a structural deficit of £3.3m over three years, significantly worse than the £2.4m forecast issued in February 2025.
findings.detail: Costs are rising at 14.1% (£1.8m) in 2026/27 while funding rises only 5.7% (£0.8m). The structural deficit grows from £1.5m in 2026/27 to £3.3m by 2029/30. The Section 151 Officer confirms this represents almost 22% of current net spending and will require 'significant transformation of services' including 'regrettable reductions in services to residents'.
findings.matters: A persistent structural deficit of this scale forces the council into unsustainable reserve drawdowns. This deterioration from the prior-year forecast signals worsening financial condition and reduced capacity to manage shocks, directly affecting the council's borrowing capacity and ability to service debt.
findings.figures: Structural deficit £1.5m (2026/27), £2.8m (2027/28), £3.2m (2028/29), £3.3m (2029/30); Costs rising £1.8m (14.1%) vs funding rising £0.8m (5.7%); prior forecast was £2.4m
findings.quote: A deficit of £3.3m represents almost 22% of current net spending and it is inevitable that savings of that scale will require a significant transformation of services, improvements in productivity and the application of modern technology alongside regrettable reductions in services to residents.

findings.headline: New Build Reserve drawn down significantly, peaking at £1.1m in 2026/27 to fund capital expenditure
findings.detail: The New Build Reserve shows planned drawdown from £43k in 2025/26 to £1,102k in 2026/27, then £760k and £740k in subsequent years. This indicates reserves are being deployed to fund capital investment rather than accumulated.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion limits the council's financial flexibility and its ability to absorb unexpected costs or fund emergency capital needs. A reserve being drawn down is only sustainable if the underlying cause (e.g., capital repayment demand) is temporary.
findings.quote: NEW BUILD RESERVE 43 1,102 760 740

findings.headline: HRA capital receipts collapse from £1.9m to £500k, a 74% reduction in a key funding source
findings.detail: Capital receipts available for HRA investment fall sharply from £1,930k in 2025/26 to £500k in 2026/27 and remain at that lower level thereafter. This represents a material reduction in internal funding capacity for housing investment going forward.
findings.matters: Capital receipts (from council house sales or asset disposals) are a finite resource. A sharp decline signals either fewer disposals anticipated or that receipts are being used elsewhere, constraining the council's future flexibility in housing investment.
findings.quote: CAPITAL RECEIPTS 1,930 500 500 500

findings.headline: General Fund borrowing requirement jumps to £3.2m in 2026/27, more than triple the prior year
findings.detail: The capital financing statement shows GF borrowing of £892k in 2025/26, rising sharply to £3,209k in 2026/27, then dropping to £2k in 2027/28. This concentration of borrowing in a single year suggests a material capital funding decision, likely driven by Levelling Up Fund projects (Rumstore £11m, public realm £5.3m) occurring in that year.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's debt trajectory and the scale of single-year borrowing decisions. A three-fold spike in borrowing in one year affects debt service costs and debt sustainability.
findings.quote: BORROWING 892 3,209 2

findings.headline: Revenue contributions to capital eliminated entirely in 2026/27, cutting off £385k funding source
findings.detail: The council's revenue contribution to capital, which stood at £385k in the revised 2025/26 budget, has been reduced to zero in 2026/27. This removes a source of capital funding at a time when overall expenditure pressures are rising.
findings.matters: Stopping revenue contributions to capital signals capital spending capacity is constrained and the council cannot afford to supplement capital investment from operational cash flow, limiting its ability to maintain or refresh infrastructure.
findings.quote: REVENUE CONTRIBUTION TO CAPITAL 641 385 -

findings.headline: Net expenditure rises 17% to £15.2m while the Revenue Financing Reserve is drawn down by £1.4m
findings.detail: Net expenditure is growing from £12,941k (revised 2025/26) to £15,204k (2026/27), an increase of £2,263k. To balance this with constrained revenues and the business rates shortfall, the council is withdrawing £1,360k from its Revenue Financing Reserve, reducing it from £3,858k to £2,498k.
findings.matters: Drawing reserves at this scale to manage recurring budget pressures is unsustainable and indicates the council is bridging a structural gap through one-time funding rather than permanent spending cuts or revenue growth.
findings.figures: 2026/27 net expenditure: £15,204k; Revenue Financing Reserve drawn down: £1,360k (35% reduction)
findings.quote: REVENUE FINANCING RESERVE B/FWD 4,674 4,086 3,858 CHANGE (783) (228) (1,360) C/FWD 3,891 3,858 2,498

findings.headline: Business rates funding projected to collapse by 64%, from £5.7m to £2.1m in 2026/27
findings.detail: Business rates income is forecast to fall from £5,714k in the revised 2025/26 budget to just £2,051k in 2026/27, a reduction of £3,663k. This represents a dramatic loss of a core, typically predictable revenue source and creates a significant funding gap.
findings.matters: Business rates are a stable, essential funding source for councils. A 64% reduction signals either a specific crisis (major business closure or revaluation) or structural deterioration in the council's rate base, both of which raise lender concerns about future revenue stability.

findings.headline: Net borrowing reduction of £9.4m to £43.4m by 30 September 2025 is explicitly temporary and cash-flow driven
findings.detail: The council's net borrowing fell sharply from £52.8m at 31 March 2025 to £43.4m by 30 September 2025, primarily through a £4.2m reduction in total debt and £5.2m increase in investments. However, the report explicitly states this is 'only a temporary position reflecting the Council's in year cash flow at this point in time', indicating the council expects net borrowing to normalise as expenditure commitments are paid during the remainder of the year.
findings.matters: This clarification is important for lenders: the improved position is not structural but timing-dependent, meaning the council's true underlying borrowing requirement remains closer to the March position.
findings.figures: Net borrowing: £52.8m (31 Mar 2025) → £43.4m (30 Sep 2025), reduction of £9.4m; total debt £54.95m (Sep) vs £59.15m (Mar)
findings.quote: At 30th September the Council had net borrowing of £43.4m a decrease of £9.4m from the 31st March 2025, this is only a temporary position reflecting the Council's in year cash flow at this point in time, this is mainly reflected in a reduction in borrowing £4.2m and increase in short term investments £5.2m.

findings.headline: General Fund financing costs ratio increased to 9.1% of net revenue from 7.1%, a 200 basis point rise despite falling interest rates
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs (capital charges net of investment income) to net revenue stream rose from a revised budget of 7.1% to an actual outturn of 9.1% for the General Fund in 2024/25. This 2 percentage point increase occurred despite Bank Rate falling from 5.25% to 4.50%, suggesting either higher debt levels or lower interest income than anticipated, indicating tighter revenue pressure from debt servicing.
findings.matters: Rising debt service costs relative to revenue constrain discretionary spending and reduce financial flexibility; this trend is counterintuitive given falling rates and warrants attention from both lenders and the finance director.
findings.figures: General Fund ratio: 7.1% revised, 9.1% actual (difference +2.0%); HRA ratio decreased from 29.5% to 28.0%
findings.quote: Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream: General Fund 7.1% (revised) 9.1% (actual) Difference 2.0%

findings.headline: Capital programme delivered £5.8m below plan across General Fund and Housing Revenue Account in 2024/25
findings.detail: General Fund capital expenditure was £6.1m against a revised budget of £10.3m (£4.3m shortfall). HRA capital expenditure was £7.8m against a revised budget of £9.4m (£1.6m shortfall). The report attributes this to slippage in the capital programme, resulting in lower unfinanced capital expenditure than planned. This affects the Capital Financing Requirement and future borrowing needs.
findings.matters: Lenders assess a council's ability to deliver its capital strategy; material underspends suggest either weak project pipeline, scope delays, or delivery risk that could indicate weaker financial management.
findings.figures: GF shortfall £4.254m; HRA shortfall £1.559m; total CFR £0.821m below estimate
findings.quote: The CFR was £0.821m less than estimated; this was mainly due to slippage with the 2024/25 capital programme which resulted in a lower level of unfinanced capital expenditure.

findings.paper_title: 01 Appendix A - Annual Governance Statement GBC 2425
findings.headline: Capacity and succession planning concerns in shared management arrangement with Portsmouth; over-reliance on key staff
findings.detail: Gosport operates shared senior management arrangements with Portsmouth City Council for Borough Treasurer, Borough Solicitor, and Strategic Head of HR. While arrangements bring cost savings and access to Portsmouth expertise, the Corporate Peer Challenge identified that this shared arrangement means these officers have limited time to focus on issues unique to Gosport. Additionally, the council has an older workforce with over-reliance on key staff in Finance and Legal, and succession planning across the council is limited—a risk to organizational resilience.
findings.matters: Over-reliance on shared key personnel and weak succession planning creates operational risk; if shared officers deprioritize Gosport issues or staff turnover occurs, finance and legal continuity could be impaired.
findings.figures: 3 shared posts (Borough Treasurer, Borough Solicitor, Strategic Head of HR) located at Portsmouth; older workforce with limited succession planning
findings.quote: The Council's Section 151 Officer (the Borough Treasurer) and Monitoring Officer (the Borough Solicitor) are both part of the shared management arrangements with Portsmouth City Council which means they have less time to focus on those issues unique to Gosport... The Council has an older workforce and there is an over-reliance on some key staff in areas such as Finance and Legal. Succession planning in key areas and across the Council is limited which is a risk for the organisation.

findings.paper_title: 01 Appendix A - Annual Governance Statement GBC 2425
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation/Devolution creates strategic uncertainty; council expects potential structural change by 2026
findings.detail: Hampshire and the Solent region has been included in the Government's Devolution Priority Programme, with elections for a Mayoral Strategic Authority expected in May 2026. Separately, the Government is inviting local government reorganisation proposals due by 21 March 2025 (detailed by 26 September 2025). Government expectation is that all two-tier areas will convert to unitary authorities with populations of at least 500,000. Gosport acknowledges no immediate implications as a borough council, but this signals potential material governance restructuring within 12-18 months.
findings.matters: Pending local government restructuring creates strategic uncertainty about the council's future governance model, funding arrangements, and service delivery structures—material for lenders evaluating long-term organizational stability.
findings.figures: Mayoral Strategic Authority elections expected May 2026, LGR detailed proposals due 26 September 2025, minimum unitary authority population 500,000
findings.quote: On 5 February 2025, the Government announced that Hampshire and The Solent will be part of the Devolution Priority Programme (DPP)... In terms of next steps for Devolution, the county council and unitary authorities will now work with the Government to establish the Hampshire and The Solent Strategic Authority, with elections for the new Mayor expected to happen in May 2026.

findings.paper_title: 01 Appendix A - Annual Governance Statement GBC 2425
findings.headline: Data protection non-compliance identified; new DPO appointed but action plan still in progress
findings.detail: The council has identified areas of non-compliance with GDPR and data retention requirements. A new Data Protection Officer was appointed in April 2025 following retirement of the previous officer. An action plan has been devised and is in process of implementation, but compliance gaps remain unresolved. This is flagged as an ongoing governance issue requiring continued monitoring.
findings.matters: GDPR non-compliance creates potential regulatory and financial liabilities; ongoing gaps with remediation still in progress suggest incomplete controls over data protection obligations.
findings.figures: New DPO appointed April 2025; action plan in progress
findings.quote: The Council has identified a number of areas with regards to data management and data retention which need to be addressed to ensure compliance with the relevant data protection legislation. An action plan has been devised and is in the process of being implemented with the recently appointed DPO.

findings.paper_title: 01 Appendix A - Annual Governance Statement GBC 2425
findings.headline: IT governance rated No Assurance; multiple IT audit failures create systemic control risk
findings.detail: 6 audits were conducted in the IT section in 2024/25; one was rated No Assurance (IT section failed to provide data) and 5 were rated Limited Assurance. This concentration of audit failures is described as a concern due to IT risks potentially causing significant disruption to the entire council. IT is not serving the council well: frequent system failures, inadequate infrastructure, inadequate equipment, and poor governance arrangements. A new Strategic Head of IT was appointed after audits concluded and reports biweekly to the Corporate Governance Group.
findings.matters: Systemic IT control failures and poor governance over IT systems create material risks to financial reporting integrity, data security, and operational continuity—all concerns for lenders evaluating organizational resilience.
findings.figures: 1 IT audit rated No Assurance, 5 IT audits rated Limited Assurance (out of 6 IT audits), representing 43% of the 44 open exceptions across the authority
findings.quote: This is a cause for concern for the Authority due to the significant number of risks raised in the department, especially as IT risks can cause significant disruption to the entire Council.

findings.paper_title: 01 Appendix A - Annual Governance Statement GBC 2425
findings.headline: Annual audit opinion downgraded to Limited Assurance; internal control framework weakening
findings.detail: The council's audit opinion has been downgraded from prior-year levels to Limited Assurance in 2024/25. Limited Assurance audits increased from 12 in 2023/24 to 17 in 2024/25. High-risk exceptions rose from 41 to 56. Most concerning: only 24% of agreed audit actions were closed in follow-ups (down from 38% in 2023/24), with 44 open or in-progress exceptions remaining across the authority. Section heads are not implementing agreed actions in timescales, indicating poor management response to identified risks.
findings.matters: A downgraded audit opinion and declining action completion rates signal weakening internal control environment and management's ineffective response to audit findings—both direct concerns for lenders assessing financial control quality and governance.
findings.figures: 17 Limited Assurance audits (up from 12 in 2023/24), 56 High Risk exceptions (up from 41), 24% of exceptions closed in 2024/25 (down from 38% in 2023/24), 44 open or in-progress exceptions
findings.quote: Based on the above results and narrative, the annual audit opinion for 2024/25 is downgraded to Limited Assurance, noting that there has been a decline in results from the previous year and a continued issue with sections implementing agreed actions in a timely manner.

findings.paper_title: 01 Appendix A - Annual Governance Statement GBC 2425
findings.headline: Council faces 3-year deficit of £2.356m and forecast reserve depletion to £1.024m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The council requires savings of £2.356m over the next 3 years, phased at £1.0m minimum for 2026/27 and £0.678m thereafter. Even with these savings and a Council Tax rise of 2.99%, the council will need to withdraw £1.291m from reserves over 2026/27-2028/29. Reserves are already being depleted £1.7m more than originally planned in 2024/25 and 2025/26 to meet unanticipated pay and contract costs, with forecast balance declining to just £1.024m in 2028/29.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's financial sustainability; a multi-year deficit, planned reserve depletion, and declining reserves to minimal levels indicates medium-term financial stress and borrowing risk.
findings.figures: £2.356m 3-year deficit, £1.0m 2026/27 savings minimum, £0.678m annual savings thereafter, £1.291m reserve withdrawal over 2026/27-2028/29, £1.024m forecast reserve balance 2028/29, £1.7m additional reserve depletion in 2024/25-2025/26
findings.quote: There is now estimated to be an overall deterioration in Reserves compared to the previous Forecast of £2.804m to the end of the Forecast period, leaving a forecast balance of just £1.024m in 2028/29.
